# MethodCache: instructions for coding agents

Copy this file into your project as agent instructions, for example as `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, a Cursor
rule, a Claude Code skill or a section of `AGENTS.md`. It tells a coding agent how to add caching with MethodCache
correctly. Full docs: https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/README.md

Bulk source reads are guarded against key, tag and clear invalidation; invalidated candidates are not published. Collection subclasses with public state are hashed with both that state and their elements. Static tags do not format arguments, and templates format only the parameters they reference.

## Adding caching to a service

1. The `MethodCache` package contains the library, the source generator and the analyzers. Nothing else is needed
   for in-memory caching.
2. Put `[Cache]` on the **interface** method, never on the class. Put `[CacheInvalidate(Tags = [...])]` on the
   interface methods that change the data. Don't change the implementation.
3. Register services as usual, then call `builder.Services.AddMethodCache()` **after** them. Later cacheable
   registrations fail at host startup or first generated binding. Missing services require explicit
   `AutoRegister(lifetime)` and exactly one accessible implementation in the selected generated module.
4. Use `MethodCacheBuilder` for startup: `Defaults`, `Group`, typed `Method`, `Memory`, `FromConfiguration`,
   `FromAssemblyOf<T>()` and the integrations' `UseRedis` / `UseSqlServer` / `UseMessagePack`. Choose a module
   explicitly when multiple assemblies generate the same interface. Keep all add-on/Core versions identical.

```cs
using MethodCache;

public interface IProductService
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:10:00", Tags = ["products", "product:{id}"])]
    Task<Product> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default);

    [Cache(Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["products"])]
    Task<List<Product>> SearchAsync(string text, int page);

    [CacheInvalidate(Tags = ["products", "product:{id}"])]
    Task UpdateAsync(int id, Product product);
}

public sealed class ProductService(Database db) : IProductService
{
    public Task<Product> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default) => db.LoadProductAsync(id, ct);

    public Task<List<Product>> SearchAsync(string text, int page) => db.SearchAsync(text, page);

    public Task UpdateAsync(int id, Product product) => db.SaveAsync(product);
}
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<Database>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();   // any lifetime
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();                               // after your registrations
```

## Rules

- Only interface methods that return a value can be cached: sync, `Task<T>` or `ValueTask<T>`. Return a list, never
  a lazy `IEnumerable<T>` or `IQueryable<T>`.
- Callers must use the interface. Calling the method from inside the class, or resolving the class itself, bypasses
  the cache.
- Keys are generated from the method and its arguments; don't write keys for `[Cache]` methods. A `CancellationToken`
  is not part of the key. Every value that changes the result must be a parameter.
- Tags take templates with a **parameter name** only: `"product:{id}"`. `"{product.Id}"` is not a template, stays
  literal and gives warning MCG015; add an `id` parameter instead. Use the same tags on the cached method and on its `[CacheInvalidate]`.
- Put ids (`int`, `Guid`) in tag templates, not free text from users: tags are plain text, so `"1:orders"` in
  `"user:{id}"` equals `"user:{id}:orders"` for id 1. Never pass passwords or tokens as arguments of cached methods.
- Durations are `TimeSpan` strings: `Duration = "00:10:00"`. Other settings: `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`
  (shorter than `Duration`), `FailSafe` (or `"off"`), `FailSafeTimeout`, `Version`, `Tags`, and a group name as the
  first argument.
- Cached objects are shared between callers: return immutable types such as records.
- For a type with only private state used as an argument or inside one (a property, a list element), implement
  `ICacheKeyProvider`.
- In library code that registers its own cached interfaces, call `AddMethodCache(null, typeof(SomeLibraryType).Assembly)`
  so the library's assembly is used, not the caller's.
- In `appsettings.json`, write durations as `"00:05:00"` (a bare number is rejected), `Tags` as a list, and only known
  setting names; anything else fails startup.
- For a client from a NuGet package with an interface, use
  `[assembly: CacheInterface(typeof(IClient), nameof(IClient.Method), Duration = "...")]` instead of a wrapper.
- Without an attribute, use `ICacheManager.GetOrCreateAsync(key, factory, o => o.WithDuration(...))` with an explicit,
  prefixed key such as `$"order:{id}"`.
- Fix every `MC` and `MCG` build diagnostic; each links to its explanation, and many have a code fix.
- In tests, register `NoOpCacheManager` (namespace `MethodCache.Extensibility`) after `AddMethodCache()` to turn
  caching off.
- To invalidate a `GetOrCreateAsync` entry that has a version, pass `CacheManagerExtensions.GetCacheKey(key, version)`
  to `InvalidateByKeysAsync`.
- For a distributed cache, use `AddMethodCacheRedis` or `AddMethodCacheSqlServer`. A custom `IDistributedCache` must
  also implement `IAtomicInvalidationStore` (`MethodCache.Extensibility`), or the app fails at startup.
- With `AddHttpCaching()`, send cookies as explicit `Cookie` headers; it turns automatic cookies off.

## Namespaces

- `MethodCache`: `[Cache]`, `[CacheInvalidate]`, `[CacheInterface]`, `ICacheManager`, `ICacheAdministrator`,
  `IRuntimeCacheConfigurator`, `MethodCacheKeys`, `MethodCacheMemoryOptions`, `Any<T>`, `ICacheKeyProvider`.
- `MethodCache.Extensibility`: `ISerializer`, `JsonCacheSerializer`, `ICacheKeyGenerator`, `JsonKeyGenerator`,
  `NoOpCacheManager`, `IAtomicInvalidationStore`.
- `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection`: `AddMethodCache`, `AddMethodCacheFromConfiguration`,
  `AddMethodCacheRedis` (package `MethodCache.Redis`), `AddMethodCacheSqlServer` (package `MethodCache.SqlServer`).

SQL backplane gap discovery remains non-blocking even for long transactions: only a separate non-waiting probe retires old missing identities. HTTP selection-rule changes retire a URL epoch once, preserving newer concurrent publications even if deletion fails after rotation. Gap failure coverage runs without infrastructure in the Core fault-injection suite, with linked SQL integration checks for real locking semantics.

# Getting started

MethodCache is not on nuget.org yet. Until it is, reference the projects from this repository (the
[demo's project file](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.Demo/MethodCache.Demo.csproj) shows how). Once published:

```bash
dotnet add package MethodCache
```

The `MethodCache` package contains the library, the source generator and the analyzers. It supports .NET 8, 9 and 10.

## 1. Start from a service

A typical service talks to a database on every call:

```cs
public sealed class ProductService(Database db)
{
    public Task<Product> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default) => db.LoadProductAsync(id, ct);

    public Task<List<Product>> SearchAsync(string text, int page) => db.SearchAsync(text, page);

    public Task UpdateAsync(int id, Product product) => db.SaveAsync(product);
}
```

## 2. Put the attributes on its interface

`[Cache]` goes on interface methods that return data, `[CacheInvalidate]` on the methods that change it. The class
only gains `: IProductService`; its methods don't change:

```cs
using MethodCache;

public interface IProductService
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:10:00", Tags = ["products", "product:{id}"])]
    Task<Product> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default);

    [Cache(Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["products"])]
    Task<List<Product>> SearchAsync(string text, int page);

    [CacheInvalidate(Tags = ["products", "product:{id}"])]
    Task UpdateAsync(int id, Product product);
}

public sealed class ProductService(Database db) : IProductService
{
    public Task<Product> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default) => db.LoadProductAsync(id, ct);

    public Task<List<Product>> SearchAsync(string text, int page) => db.SearchAsync(text, page);

    public Task UpdateAsync(int id, Product product) => db.SaveAsync(product);
}
```

- `GetAsync(42)` is stored for ten minutes under a key built from the method and its argument
  (`...IProductService.GetAsync:42`). The `CancellationToken` is not part of the key.
- `"product:{id}"` is a tag template: `GetAsync(42)` is tagged `product:42`.
- `UpdateAsync(42, ...)` removes every entry tagged `products` or `product:42` once it has completed.

The attributes must be on the interface. On a class they do nothing, and the analyzer reports
[MC0001](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0001) with a code fix that moves them.

## 3. Register it

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<Database>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();   // any lifetime
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();                               // after your registrations
```

`AddMethodCache()` wraps every registered interface that has cached methods in its generated decorator and keeps the
lifetime you chose. Register cacheable services before this call. A later cacheable registration fails at host
startup, or when a generated decorator first binds without a host. Unrelated services may be registered later.
Calling `AddMethodCache` again decorates newly added services and keeps existing decorators intact.

Missing implementations are registered only with explicit `AutoRegister(ServiceLifetime.Scoped)` (or another
lifetime). Select the generated module with `FromAssemblyOf<ProductService>()`; exactly one accessible concrete
implementation must exist for each missing service. Zero or multiple candidates give an error naming the service,
module and candidates. Explicit DI registrations always retain their implementation and lifetime.

When multiple assemblies generate decorators for the same interface, select one module with
`FromAssemblyOf<SomeTypeInThatAssembly>()`. No entry-assembly or alphabetical preference is applied. The same
module selection and candidate data work under JIT and Native AOT.

Keyed registrations (`AddKeyedScoped<IProductService, ProductService>("primary")`) are cached too, under the same
key; an interface registered only keyed is not also registered without a key. The service key is part of the cache
keys, so each keyed registration of an interface caches its own results; it must be a string, enum, bool, char,
integer or `Guid` ([Keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md#things-to-know)). A catch-all registration with `KeyedService.AnyKey` is
rejected, since its implementation is created for whichever key is requested; register concrete keys instead.
Open generic registrations and closed types without a generated binding also give a named startup error.

Generic interfaces work the same way: `IRepository<User>` is cached for every closed type a class in your project
implements, such as `UserRepository : IRepository<User>`. An open generic registration such as
`AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(Repository<>))` is not cached; register the closed types instead.

### Registering with a factory

A factory registration is cached like any other: register it before `AddMethodCache()`, and the decorator wraps
what your factory returns, with the lifetime you chose.

```cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService>(
    sp => new ProductService(sp.GetRequiredService<Database>()));
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

## What can be cached

```cs
[Cache] Product Get(int id);                          // synchronous
[Cache] Task<Product> GetAsync(int id);               // Task<T>
[Cache] ValueTask<Product> GetFastAsync(int id);      // ValueTask<T>
[Cache] Task<Product?> FindAsync(string name);        // null results are cached too
```

- Synchronous methods, `Task<T>` and `ValueTask<T>` can be cached. A method that returns nothing has nothing to
  cache, so `[Cache]` on it is a build error ([MCG001](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg001),
  [MCG002](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg002)). So is a lazy `IEnumerable<T>` or `IQueryable<T>`
  ([MCG014](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg014)): return a list.
  Synchronous methods use L1/origin when the distributed adapter has no bounded native synchronous capability.
  Custom async-only managers bypass their synchronous caching path; see [Generated decorators](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/source-generator.md).
- Exceptions are never cached: the next call runs the method again.
- Concurrent calls with the same arguments share one call to your method (stampede protection). A caller that cancels
  only stops its own wait.
- Without a `Duration`, entries live five minutes (`MethodCacheMemoryOptions.DefaultExpiration`) unless you set a
  default ([Expiration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md#duration)).
- `null` results are cached. Turn that off with `CacheNullValues` on the [memory cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/memory-cache.md), or
  per method with [conditional caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md).
- The cached object is returned as is, not copied. Treat cached results as read-only.

## Next steps

- Choose how long entries live: [Expiration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md).
- Remove entries when data changes: [Invalidation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md).
- Change durations without a redeploy: [Configuration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md).
- Share the cache between instances: [Distributed cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/source-generator.md -->

# Generated decorators

Put cache attributes on interface methods. The generator builds a decorator around the registered implementation
and routes cached calls through MethodCache. Your implementation stays ordinary application code.

The generator supports synchronous result methods, `Task<T>` and `ValueTask<T>`, overloaded methods, generic
interfaces and generic methods, including interfaces nested in generic containing types. Constraints on both
the containing type and the interface, including `unmanaged` and base class constraints, are preserved, and so are
`scoped` parameters on forwarded members. Each overload has its own
[method id](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#appsettingsjson) and its own cache entries.

Public interface members are forwarded to the implementation: uncached methods, properties, indexers and events.
Non-public and sealed default interface methods stay on the interface with their own bodies; the decorator doesn't
implement them, so `[Cache]` or `[CacheInvalidate]` on one (or on a `static` member) is warning
[MCG017](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg017). An interface with non-public abstract members is rejected with
[MCG013](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg013), because the decorator can't call those members on the implementation.

Keywords and unusual names are escaped, and your own types named like framework types (such as `Task` or `List`)
don't clash with the generated code. You don't need to rename anything.

Unsupported cached method shapes receive a [generator diagnostic](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md), with a code fix
to remove the cache attribute where available. Reference returns, ref struct results and pointer/function pointer
results are rejected before cached code is emitted. Those methods are forwarded when another method on the
interface is cacheable. See [keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md) for argument identity and
[configuration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md) for generated policy identifiers.

## Registration

Generated runtime calls use the versioned `MethodCache.Generated` facade. Module initializers record descriptors
only; `AddMethodCache` validates contract versions before executing descriptors or factories. Each invocation
captures one immutable policy/prefix/publication generation, including keyed registration and background-scope
binding. A retired invocation may finish its origin call but cannot publish into the current generation.

`AddMethodCache()` wraps every registration of a cached interface in its decorator, and keeps the container's
ownership as it is: the container disposes the implementations it creates, and leaves instances you registered
yourself open. Factory registrations are wrapped the same way ([Getting started](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#registering-with-a-factory)).

A factory registration for the README's `IUserService`, once `IUserDatabase` is registered:

```cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<IUserService>(sp =>
    new UserService(sp.GetRequiredService<IUserDatabase>()));
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

The end-to-end signature corpus under `tests/MethodCache.SourceGenerator.IntegrationTests` checks supported shapes
with C# 12 and the latest compiler: each generated decorator compiles and runs through the actual DI registration.
It checks semantic runtime references as well. Frozen vendor binaries exercise contract compatibility without
regenerating source during ordinary tests, including under Native AOT.

`AddMethodCache` decorates explicit registrations. Missing services require explicit `AutoRegister(lifetime)`
with exactly one accessible implementation in the selected module. Use `FromAssemblyOf<T>()` when multiple
modules offer the same interface. Cacheable late, open generic, AnyKey and unsupported closed bindings fail explicitly.

Built-in synchronous methods run a synchronous factory with synchronous single-flight. They never wait on an
async loader or async refresh. Async callers can join a synchronous load. A custom async-only manager bypasses
synchronous caching and emits a diagnostic once per method/container. Current distributed adapters do not expose
bounded native synchronous operations through this path, so these calls use L1/origin and report unavailable L2;
use async methods to share results through L2. Synchronous distributed tag mutations report unsupported invalidation
after the origin/local mutation; use async mutation methods for distributed invalidation.

The attribute-move code fix preserves semantic binding across scopes and files: attribute/type aliases are qualified as needed, and constant arguments are materialized before they leave an implementation class.

On C# 13/.NET 9 or newer, generated decorators preserve `allows ref struct` constraints when the cached values and arguments themselves are ordinary cacheable types. Potentially ref-like type parameters used as cache arguments or results receive MCG007 instead of broken generated code. The generator still supports the .NET 8 compiler baseline.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/keys.md -->

# Cache keys

You never write keys for `[Cache]` methods. The generated decorator builds each key from the interface, the method
and the arguments, so two calls share an entry exactly when they call the same method with equal arguments.

```cs
public sealed record UserQuery(string Name, int Page);

public interface IUserService
{
    [Cache] Task<User> GetAsync(int id);                     // MyApp.IUserService.GetAsync:42
    [Cache] Task<List<User>> SearchAsync(UserQuery query);   // MyApp.IUserService.SearchAsync:(alice:2)
    [Cache] Task<List<User>> ByIdsAsync(int[] ids);          // MyApp.IUserService.ByIdsAsync:[3:1:2:3]
    [Cache] Task<int> CountAsync(Dictionary<string, int[]> filters); // MyApp.IUserService.CountAsync:fc08ab0d… (hashed)
}
```

## How arguments become keys

- **Simple values** (strings, numbers, `bool`, `Guid`, dates, enums) are written as they are: `GetAsync:42`.
- **Records, classes and structs** whose public properties and fields are simple values are written field by field:
  `SearchAsync:(alice:2)`. Two records with equal values give the same key.
- **Types that implement `ICacheKeyProvider`** contribute their `CacheKeyPart`.
- **Arrays and collections** of those values are written with their count and then each element in order:
  `ByIdsAsync:[3:1:2:3]`. Records and classes inside a collection must be sealed, since an unsealed element type
  could hold a subclass with more members. A dictionary counts when its keys and values are simple values. When a
  collection's runtime type differs from its declared type (an array or a list passed as `IEnumerable<int>`), the key
  includes that type, so an array and a list with the same elements stay two entries. Unknown collection subclasses passed through a base class or interface use the key generator so their own runtime state is preserved.
- **Collection subclasses with public state**, such as a list with a tenant or scope property, use the key generator. Their keys include both that public state and the elements, including when the collection is behind a base-class property. This applies to the default, JSON and MessagePack key generators.
- **Everything else**, such as an interface or `object` argument or a collection of collections, goes through the key
  generator. The default, `FastHashKeyGenerator`, hashes the arguments into a key such as `CountAsync:fc08ab0d…`.
- **Framework types** are written by their value wherever they appear, not by their public properties; see
  [Framework types](#framework-types). Other framework types are a build error.
- **`nint` and `nuint`** also go through the key generator, as the 64-bit number they hold, so a value gets the same
  key in 32-bit and 64-bit processes. Their type is kept: `(nint)1`, `1` and `1L` are three keys, also inside an
  `object[]` or an `object` property.
- **Values inside hashed arguments keep their runtime type.** Where a value's type differs from the type it is declared
  as (an element of `object[]` or `List<object>`, an `object` property, a property typed as a base class or interface),
  the key records the value's type and all of its members: `new object[] { 1 }` and `new object[] { 1L }` get
  different keys, and so do two `Circle`s behind a `Shape` property that differ only in `Radius`.
- A `CancellationToken` parameter is never part of the key.
- Keys don't depend on the current culture: `-1`, `1.5` and dates are written the same under every culture.
- `0.0` and `-0.0` are two keys in every key form (`1 / x` tells them apart). `NaN` and the infinities work anywhere,
  also inside a hashed argument, such as `double.PositiveInfinity` as a "no limit" value in a filter record.

On .NET 9 and later the decorator writes simple keys into a stack buffer and looks them up without allocating.

## Types whose state is private

A type with only private state, including private fields inherited from a base class, would give every value the
same key, so the key generators refuse it with an
`InvalidOperationException` instead of returning wrong results. This holds wherever the type appears in an argument:
as the argument itself, as a property of a record, or as an element of an array, list or dictionary. Implement
`ICacheKeyProvider` on it, or give it public properties:

```cs
public sealed class TenantId(Guid value) : ICacheKeyProvider
{
    private readonly Guid _value = value;   // private state: MethodCache can't see it

    public string CacheKeyPart => _value.ToString("N");
}
```

## Framework types

Types from .NET itself often keep their value out of their public properties (`BigInteger` has `IsZero` and
`Sign`, `IPAddress.ScopeId` throws for IPv4), so writing those would give different values one key. These go through
the key generator, which writes their value, in an argument of their own or inside a record, collection or tuple:

- `Guid`, `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `TimeSpan`, `DateOnly`, `TimeOnly`
- `Half`, `Int128`, `UInt128`, `BigInteger`, `Complex`
- `Uri`, `Version`, `IPAddress` (`IPAddress.Loopback` and `IPAddress.Parse("127.0.0.1")` share a key)
- `JsonElement`, as its JSON, so `{"a":1}` and `{ "a": 1 }` share a key
- `Index`, `Range`, `Vector2`, `Vector3`, `Vector4`, `Quaternion`, `Plane`, `Matrix3x2`, `Matrix4x4`
- ASP.NET Core's `PathString`, `QueryString` and `HostString`
- arrays, collections, `Memory<T>`, `Tuple`, `ValueTuple` and `KeyValuePair` of these

Any other type from .NET itself, ASP.NET Core or Microsoft.Extensions in a key (one from an assembly named
`System.*`, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.*` or `Microsoft.Extensions.*`), such as `StringBuilder` (which can change after
the call), `CultureInfo`, `Stream`, `Type` or a delegate, is build error
[MCG018](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg018), also as a property of your own record. Pass a value that identifies
it, such as `culture.Name`, or wrap it in a type that implements `ICacheKeyProvider`. Other libraries' models, such
as an SDK's classes in a `Microsoft.*` namespace, are written by their public properties like your own types.

## Readable keys while debugging

`JsonKeyGenerator` writes the arguments it handles as JSON (for example `[42,"alice"]`) instead of a hash:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<ICacheKeyGenerator, JsonKeyGenerator>());
```

The JSON is followed by a short hash of the arguments' runtime types (`[42,"alice"]:9c41…`), so arguments that
write the same JSON, such as `1` and `1L` or two classes with the same properties, still get different keys. A value
inside an argument whose type differs from its declared type is written with its type, for example
`[{"\uFFFFt":"System.Int64","v":1}]` for `new object[] { 1L }`.

Both generators are in `MethodCache.Extensibility`. Keys built by the decorator itself (simple values, records,
`ICacheKeyProvider`) don't change with the generator.

## Using an argument as the key

`[CacheKey(UseAsRawKey = true)]` on a parameter makes that argument the whole key. The interface, the method name, the
`Version` and the other arguments are not part of it:

```cs
public interface IDocumentStore
{
    // The argument is the whole key: GetAsync("doc:2026/report.pdf") is stored as "doc:2026/report.pdf"
    [Cache] Task<byte[]> GetAsync([CacheKey(UseAsRawKey = true)] string key);
}
```

Strings are used as they are. Dates are written as in generated keys (`MethodCacheKeys.Part`), in the round-trip
format (`2026-01-01T12:00:00.2500000Z`): fractions of a second and a `DateTimeOffset`'s offset are part of the key,
and a local `DateTime` is written as UTC, so the key doesn't depend on the server's time zone and a local time and the
UTC time of the same instant share an entry. Numbers and other formattable values are written in the invariant culture;
any other type uses its own `ToString()`, so make sure that doesn't depend on the current culture. The key is not escaped and has no
prefix, so two methods, or a `GetOrCreateAsync` call, that produce the same text share one entry. Use it only for keys
your own code builds, never for text a caller controls; see [Security](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/security.md).

## Building a key yourself

`MethodCacheKeys` builds the key the decorator uses, so you can invalidate or inspect one entry without guessing the
format:

```cs
var key = MethodCacheKeys.For(typeof(IOrderService), nameof(IOrderService.GetAsync), MethodCacheKeys.Part(42));
await cache.InvalidateByKeysAsync(key);   // "Docs.Invalidation.IOrderService.GetAsync:42"
```

For a method with a `Version`, use `MethodCacheKeys.ForVersion`. For an overloaded method, pass its
[method id](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#appsettingsjson) as the name, such as `FindAsync(string)`:

```cs
// A method with a Version: "MyApp.IInvoiceService.GetAsync:v2:42"
var versioned = MethodCacheKeys.ForVersion(
    typeof(IInvoiceService), nameof(IInvoiceService.GetAsync), 2, MethodCacheKeys.Part(42));

// An overloaded method: pass its method id. "MyApp.IInvoiceService.FindAsync(string):INV-7"
var overload = MethodCacheKeys.For(
    typeof(IInvoiceService), "FindAsync(string)", MethodCacheKeys.Part("INV-7"));
```

`MethodCacheKeys.Prefix(type, name, version)` returns the start that every key of one method shares, for example for
`ICacheAdministrator.ListEntries(keyPrefix: ...)`. `MethodCacheKeys.Pattern` returns the same followed by `*`.

## Things to know

- **Keys contain the arguments.** Don't cache methods that take secrets such as passwords or tokens as arguments; pass
  an identifier instead. Hashed keys are not encryption. No argument, whatever characters it contains, can produce
  another call's key; see [Security](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/security.md).
- **`Version` changes every key** of a method, so values cached by an earlier version are ignored. See
  [Expiration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md#versions).
- **Overloaded methods** have their parameter types in their keys, so overloads never share entries. See
  [method ids](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#appsettingsjson).
- **A method name that another interface in the hierarchy also declares** gets the same treatment. Keys start with
  the decorated interface, so for `ICatalog : ILookup` with `ILookup.Find(int)` and `ICatalog.Find(string)` the keys
  are `MyApp.ICatalog.Find(int):7` and `MyApp.ICatalog.Find(string):7`. When two base interfaces declare the same
  signature, the declaring interface is added too: for `IC : IA, IB` that both declare `Get(int)`, the keys are
  `MyApp.IC.MyApp.IA.Get(int):1` and `MyApp.IC.MyApp.IB.Get(int):1`. Policy ids don't change; each
  method keeps the id of the interface that declares it.
- **Keyed registrations** have their service key after the method name, so `AddKeyedScoped<IRates, EcbRates>("ecb")`
  and `AddKeyedScoped<IRates, FedRates>("fed")` each cache their own results: `MyApp.IRates.Get@ecb:1` and
  `MyApp.IRates.Get@fed:1`. `MethodCacheKeys.KeyedMethodName("Get", "ecb")` returns the name to pass to `For`,
  `Prefix` or `Pattern`. Other keys carry their type (`Get@MyApp.Region.Eu`, `Get@Int32(7)`), and a string with a
  `.`, `(` or `"` in it is written in quotes, so keys of different types never share entries. The service key must be a string, enum, bool, char, integer or `Guid`; `AddMethodCache()`
  throws for a keyed registration of a cached interface with any other key. A `KeyedService.AnyKey` registration is
  left uncached. `MethodCacheKeys.Pattern(type, "Get")`
  matches the entries of every registration. Tags don't include the service key, so a `[CacheInvalidate]` tag, on any
  registration, removes the matching entries of all of them.
- To see the keys your application produces, list them with `ICacheAdministrator.ListEntries()` or the admin
  endpoints ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

MessagePack keys preserve derived member data in nested base-class/interface slots and collection elements. Earlier keys for these arguments change; existing entries become cold misses and expire normally.

Overloaded generic methods include generic arity in their policy ids and key prefixes: `Get(int)`, `Get``1(int)` and `Get``2(int)` remain distinct. Generator and runtime configuration use the same ids; earlier keys for overloaded generic methods become cold misses.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/expiration.md -->

# Expiration

Each cached method decides how long its entries live. The settings below can be set on `[Cache]`, in startup code, in
`appsettings.json` or at runtime ([Configuration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md)).

```cs
public interface IReportService
{
    // Gone ten minutes after it was stored
    [Cache(Duration = "00:10:00")]
    Task<Report> GetAsync(int year);

    // Kept while it is read at least every five minutes, but never longer than an hour
    [Cache(Duration = "01:00:00", SlidingExpiration = "00:05:00")]
    Task<Session> GetSessionAsync(string id);

    // Reloaded in the background when it is read in its last minute, so callers never wait
    [Cache(Duration = "00:10:00", RefreshAhead = "00:01:00")]
    Task<PriceList> GetPricesAsync(string region);

    // Changing the version changes every key, so values cached by the previous version are ignored
    [Cache(Duration = "1.00:00:00", Version = 2)]
    Task<Report> GetYearlyAsync(int year);
}
```

Time spans use the `TimeSpan` format: `"00:05:00"` is five minutes, `"01:00:00"` an hour, `"1.00:00:00"` a day. A
value that isn't a positive time span is a build error ([MC0004](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0004)).

## Duration

`Duration` is how long an entry lives after it was stored. A method without one uses the global default:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config =>
    config.Defaults(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15))));
```

Without any default, entries live for `MethodCacheMemoryOptions.DefaultExpiration` (five minutes). No entry lives
longer than `MethodCacheMemoryOptions.MaxExpiration` (seven days). See [Memory cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/memory-cache.md).

## Sliding expiration

`SlidingExpiration` keeps an entry while it is read: each read extends its life by the sliding window. It never lives
past its `Duration`; without a `Duration`, only `MaxExpiration` limits it.

## Refresh-ahead

`RefreshAhead` reloads an entry in the background when it is read within that window before it expires. The caller
gets the cached value at once, and the reload replaces it, so a popular entry never makes anyone wait. An entry that
isn't read in the window simply expires.

The window must be shorter than `Duration` and `SlidingExpiration`, or every read would reload the entry: in code
(`Build()` throws an `InvalidOperationException`) and in `appsettings.json` (startup fails) a longer one is rejected.
When settings from different places combine into such a window, for example an attribute's `RefreshAhead` with a
shorter `Duration` from configuration, the reload starts halfway through the entry's life instead.

The reload outlives the request that triggered it. For a service registered as scoped or transient (a repository
with a scoped `DbContext`, say), it runs on a new instance from a new DI scope, which is disposed when the reload ends,
never on the request's instance, whose scope may already be gone. That instance has none of the request's state: no
`HttpContext`, and no values the request set on the instance or in `AsyncLocal`. Each scoped or transient cached
service the reload calls gets an instance this way, also from a manual `GetOrCreateAsync` factory, and every scope is
disposed when the reload ends; a call the factory leaves running after it returned keeps the instance it was given.
Singletons reload on their one instance. A `CancellationToken` parameter of the method still cancels the reload.

## Versions

`Version` is part of every key the method produces. Raise it when the shape of the cached result changes, for example
after adding a property, so values cached by the previous deployment are never returned. The old entries expire on
their own.

## Spreading out expiry

Entries created at the same moment, for example right after a deploy, also expire together.
`MethodCacheMemoryOptions.JitterMaxDuration` adds a random extra lifetime to each entry to spread them out
([Memory cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/memory-cache.md)).

## Removing entries early

Expiration is for data that may be a little old. When you know data changed, remove it right away with
[invalidation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/invalidation.md -->

# Invalidation

Expiration removes entries eventually; invalidation removes them the moment you know the data changed.

## Tags

Give cached methods tags, and list the same tags on the methods that change the data:

```cs
public interface IOrderService
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:10:00", Tags = ["orders", "order:{orderId}"])]
    Task<Order> GetAsync(int orderId);

    [Cache(Duration = "00:05:00", Tags = ["orders", "customer:{customerId}:orders"])]
    Task<List<Order>> ListForCustomerAsync(int customerId);

    // Removes this order and the customer's list, nothing else
    [CacheInvalidate(Tags = ["order:{orderId}", "customer:{customerId}:orders"])]
    Task CancelAsync(int orderId, int customerId);

    // Removes every cached order
    [CacheInvalidate(Tags = ["orders"])]
    Task ImportAsync(Stream file);
}
```

- `[CacheInvalidate]` removes every entry with any of its tags once the method has completed successfully. If it
  throws, nothing is removed.
- A tag can be shared by many methods, so one write clears every cached view of the same data.
- `[CacheInvalidate]` without tags removes nothing and is reported as [MCG005](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg005).

## Tag templates

`"order:{orderId}"` is filled in from the method's arguments: `GetAsync(42)` is tagged `order:42`, and
`CancelAsync(42, 7)` removes `order:42`. The name in braces must be a parameter of the method it is on. The exact
spelling is used first; otherwise a single case-insensitive match is used. A name that matches several parameters
only by case, such as `{NAME}` for `name` and `Name`, stays literal text and is reported as
[MCG016](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg016). An unknown name is reported as
[MCG009](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg009), with a code fix that offers the closest parameter. An argument's text is inserted as it is, even if it contains braces: an id of `"{org}"` gives
the tag `order:{org}` on both the cached call and the invalidation.

A template takes a parameter name only. `"{order.Id}"` is not a template and stays literal text, so every call would
share one tag; it is reported as [MCG015](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg015). Add the id as a parameter, as `UpdateAsync(int id, Product product)` does in
[Getting started](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md).

Static tags never format method arguments. A template formats only the parameters it references, in the invariant culture; an unrelated argument's `ToString()` is not invoked.

Tags set in startup code, `appsettings.json` or runtime overrides can use templates too, with any parameter of the
method. They are added to the `[Cache]` attribute's tags, so the attribute's `[CacheInvalidate]` tags keep working;
only an explicit `ClearTags()` (or `"ClearTags": true` in `appsettings.json`) replaces them
([Configuration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md)). An override with `o => o.WithTags("incident")` on `GetAsync` above gives its
entries the tags `orders`, `order:{orderId}` and `incident`.

`[CacheInvalidate]` also works on methods with `ref` or `ref readonly` returns, and on `Task` and `ValueTask` methods
with `ref`, `out` or `in` parameters. The tags are filled in after the call returns, and the entries are removed only
once the task has completed successfully.

## From code

`ICacheManager` invalidates by tag, by key or by pattern:

```cs
await cache.InvalidateByTagsAsync("order:42", "customer:7:orders");
```

```cs
var key = MethodCacheKeys.For(typeof(IOrderService), nameof(IOrderService.GetAsync), MethodCacheKeys.Part(42));
await cache.InvalidateByKeysAsync(key);   // "Docs.Invalidation.IOrderService.GetAsync:42"
```

```cs
await cache.InvalidateByTagPatternAsync("customer:7:*");   // in-memory cache only
```

- `MethodCacheKeys.For` builds the key the generated decorator uses. Versioned and overloaded methods need a little
  more; see [Building a key yourself](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md#building-a-key-yourself).
- Patterns match tags, with `*` for any number of characters and `?` for one. With a distributed cache configured,
  `InvalidateByTagPatternAsync` throws `NotSupportedException`, because the distributed cache can't list its tags;
  invalidate exact tags instead.
- The admin endpoints and `ICacheAdministrator` also invalidate by tag ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

## With several instances

With [Redis or SQL Server](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md), invalidating a tag or key removes it from the distributed cache and
tells every instance to drop its in-memory copy. You don't need to do anything else.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/fail-safe.md -->

# Fail-safe

Fail-safe keeps an expired value for a while and returns it when calling the method again fails, so a database or API
outage shows slightly old data instead of errors. It is off by default.

## Turning it on

For every cached method at once:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config => config.Defaults(o => o.FailSafe(
    duration: TimeSpan.FromHours(1),              // how long an expired value is kept as a fallback
    timeout: TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),      // optional: don't wait longer than this when a fallback exists
    retryAfter: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))));       // optional: reuse the fallback this long before trying again
```

or in `appsettings.json`:

```json
{
  "MethodCache": {
    "FailSafe": { "Duration": "01:00:00", "Timeout": "00:00:00.200", "RetryAfter": "00:00:30" }
  }
}
```

## What happens

- **When the method throws**, the caller gets the expired value if it is younger than `duration`. That value is then
  reused for `retryAfter` (default 30 seconds) before the method is called again, so a failing dependency isn't
  hammered; no [refresh-ahead](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md#refresh-ahead) reload starts during that time either.
- **When the method is slow** and `timeout` is set, the caller gets the expired value after `timeout` and the call
  finishes in the background; its result replaces the old value. Without an expired value the caller waits as usual.
  Because the call may outlive the request, a scoped or transient service makes it on a new instance from a new DI
  scope, disposed when the call ends, whenever a fallback exists and `timeout` is set (the instance has none of the
  request's own state, such as values set on the instance). The caller's `HttpContext` and `AsyncLocal` values still
  flow to it, as it starts on the caller's call. Singletons use their one instance.
- A caller's own cancellation is never treated as a failure, so it doesn't trigger fail-safe.
- A value that was invalidated (its key, a tag or a clear) or replaced is never a fallback, also when that happened
  while the reload ran: callers then wait for the reload, or get its exception.
- Without an expired value, the exception reaches the caller as usual.

## Per method

A method or group can change any of it, and its own setting wins over the central one. The retry interval can be set
in code or `appsettings.json` only, not on `[Cache]`:

```cs
public interface IAccountService
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:05:00", FailSafe = "01:00:00", FailSafeTimeout = "00:00:00.200")]
    Task<Rates> GetRatesAsync();

    [Cache(FailSafe = "off")]   // a balance must never be old, so an error is better
    Task<decimal> GetBalanceAsync(int accountId);
}
```

In code, use the same builder method: `Configure(o => o.FailSafe(TimeSpan.FromHours(1)))`. `o.FailSafe(TimeSpan.Zero)`
turns it off. In `appsettings.json`, a method takes `FailSafe` (a time span or `"off"`), `FailSafeTimeout` and
`FailSafeRetryAfter`.

## Limits

The fallback lives in each instance's memory, so right after a restart there is none until the method has succeeded
once.

Caller cancellation stops the wait during an L2 read or a slow factory, including bulk reads and fail-safe waits. L2 reads pass cancellation to the backend; shared factory work may finish for other callers. Caller cancellation is not reported as a dependency failure.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/conditional-caching.md -->

# Conditional caching

Sometimes a result should be returned but not remembered: an empty search, a product that doesn't exist yet, a
response that says "try again later".

## CacheWhen

`CacheWhen` stores a result only when the predicate returns true:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config =>
{
    // Don't remember empty search results: the next search asks the database again
    config.Method((IProductService s) => s.SearchAsync(Any<string>.Value))
          .CacheWhen(results => results.Count > 0);

    // A product that doesn't exist yet may be created any moment
    config.Method((IProductService s) => s.FindAsync(Any<int>.Value))
          .CacheWhen(product => product is not null);
});
```

- A rejected result is still returned to the caller, and the next call runs the method again.
- The entry it would have replaced, including a fail-safe value, stays.
- The predicate runs once per load, never on a cache hit. If it throws, the result is returned and not stored.
- It is set in startup code only, so it can't come from `appsettings.json`. `Any<T>.Value` stands for any argument.

To stop caching `null` everywhere, set `CacheNullValues = false` on the [memory cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/memory-cache.md) instead.

## Skipping the cache for one call

With [manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md), `When` decides per call whether to use the cache at all:

```cs
var results = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"search:{text}",
    async (ctx, ct) => await search(),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10))
          .When(ctx => !preview));   // preview requests skip the cache entirely
```

When the predicate returns false, the factory runs and its result is neither read from nor written to the cache.
`When` only applies to `GetOrCreateAsync`; for a `[Cache]` method use `CacheWhen`
([Validation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#validation)).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/configuration.md -->

# Configuration

A cached method's policy (duration, sliding expiration, refresh-ahead, fail-safe, tags, group, version) can come from
four layers. Change it in `appsettings.json` or at runtime, and the next call uses it, without a redeploy.

| Layer | How you set it | Priority | Changes while running |
|-------|----------------|----------|-----------------------|
| Attributes | `[Cache(...)]` on the interface method | 10 (lowest) | No |
| Startup code | `AddMethodCache(config => ...)` | 40 | No |
| Configuration | `AddMethodCacheFromConfiguration(configuration)` | 50 | Yes, when the configuration reloads |
| Runtime overrides | `IRuntimeCacheConfigurator` | 100 (highest) | Yes |

When several layers configure the same method, they are merged setting by setting, and the highest layer that sets a
setting wins. A runtime override of `Duration` leaves the attribute's `Tags` in place.

Tags are the exception: they are combined, not replaced. Tags from startup code, `appsettings.json`, runtime overrides
and the defaults are added to the `[Cache]` attribute's tags (without duplicates), so a `[CacheInvalidate]` that
lists an attribute tag always reaches the entry. To replace the tags instead, call `ClearTags()` before `WithTags`
(`o => o.ClearTags().WithTags("orders")`), or set `"ClearTags": true` next to `Tags` for a method in
`appsettings.json`. The tags of the lower layers and of the defaults are then dropped, and an entry without them is
no longer removed by a `[CacheInvalidate]` that lists them.

## Defaults and groups

Within the layers, each setting comes from the most specific place that sets it: the method itself, then its group,
then the defaults.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config =>
{
    // Every cached method: fills in what the method leaves unset
    config.Defaults(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15)));

    // Methods in the "user-data" group: [Cache("user-data")] or WithGroup("user-data")
    config.Group("user-data", o => o.WithSlidingExpiration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)));

    // One method
    config.Method((IUserService s) => s.GetProfileAsync(Any<int>.Value))
          .Configure(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)).RefreshAhead(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)));
});
```

- `Defaults` applies to every cached method, also ones that only have `[Cache]`. `[Cache(Duration = "00:10:00")]`
  keeps its ten minutes while the defaults fill in what it leaves out.
- A method joins a group with `[Cache("name")]`, `WithGroup("name")` in code, or `Group` in `appsettings.json`.
- `Any<T>.Value` stands for any argument when you point at a method.

Startup uses `MethodCacheBuilder`: `Defaults`, `Group`, typed `Method` expressions, `Memory`,
`FromConfiguration`, `FromAssemblyOf` and explicit `AutoRegister(lifetime)`. Redis, SQL Server and MessagePack
packages add `UseRedis`, `UseSqlServer` and `UseMessagePack`; Core provides `UseJson`.
All integration packages require the exact same Core package version; do not override this bound.
CI uses strict restore (NU1608 as an error) to reject direct-version overrides. Configure services before `AddMethodCache`.
Runtime override methods retain their separate policy API; the builder configures startup only.

## appsettings.json

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddMethodCacheFromConfiguration(builder.Configuration);   // the "MethodCache" section
```

```json
{
  "MethodCache": {
    "Defaults": { "Duration": "00:15:00" },
    "FailSafe": { "Duration": "01:00:00" },
    "Services": {
      "MyApp.IUserService.GetProfileAsync": {
        "Duration": "01:00:00",
        "SlidingExpiration": "00:10:00",
        "RefreshAhead": "00:05:00",
        "Tags": ["users"],
        "Version": 1,
        "Notes": "Profiles change rarely"
      },
      "MyApp.IAccountService.GetBalanceAsync": { "FailSafe": "off" }
    }
  }
}
```

- Each key under `Services` is the **method id**: the full name of the interface, a dot and the method name. A generic
  interface is written with its type parameters (`MyApp.IRepository<T>.GetAsync`), and an overloaded method adds its
  parameter types (`MyApp.IUserService.FindAsync(int)`). Parameter types other than built-in ones are qualified by
  namespace (`MyApp.IUsers.Find(MyApp.Request)`), so overloads taking `A.Request` and `B.Request` stay separate. Types
  are named as reflection sees them: a tuple is `System.ValueTuple<int, string>` (element names dropped), `nint` is
  `System.IntPtr` and `dynamic` is `object`. Runtime overrides by method id use the same format, and the parameter
  list is also part of the method's cache keys. The admin endpoints list every method id ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).
- Settings: `Duration`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`, `FailSafe` (a time span or `"off"`), `FailSafeTimeout`,
  `FailSafeRetryAfter`, `Tags`, `Version`, `Group`, `Metadata` and `Notes`, plus `ClearTags` (`true` or `false`) for a
  method under `Services`: `true` makes its `Tags` replace the attribute's instead of adding to them. `Metadata` and `Notes` are recorded for
  diagnostics and don't change caching. Names are case-insensitive; any other name is an error, so a misspelled
  `"Durration"` is reported instead of ignored. The same goes for the section itself: it holds only `Defaults`,
  `FailSafe` and `Services`.
- Time spans are written `"hh:mm:ss"` (or `"d.hh:mm:ss"`); a bare number such as `"300"` is rejected, since .NET
  would read it as 300 days. `Tags` is a list (`["users"]`), and a method's `FailSafe` is one time span: the
  `{ "Duration", "Timeout", "RetryAfter" }` block exists only at the top of the section.
- A method can also be listed under an index with a `MethodId` property. Environment variable names can't hold `.`,
  `(` or `<`, so this is how environment variables, Kubernetes `env` or Linux App Service configure a method:

  ```bash
  MethodCache__Services__0__MethodId="MyApp.IUserService.FindAsync(int)"
  MethodCache__Services__0__Duration="00:02:00"
  ```
- `Defaults` applies to every cached method; the top-level `FailSafe` section is described in [Fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md).
- Pass a section name as the second argument to read another section. Environment files such as
  `appsettings.Production.json` work as usual. The section is read when the host starts, so configuration sources
  added after `AddMethodCacheFromConfiguration`, such as a later `AddJsonFile` or a `WebApplicationFactory`'s test
  settings, apply from the first call.
- Changes apply while the application runs, as soon as the configuration reloads (`appsettings.json` reloads on save
  by default).
- Only methods with `[Cache]` (or listed in `[assembly: CacheInterface]`) have a decorator, so the file can change
  their policy but can't make other methods cached. A method id that matches no cached method, such as a misspelled
  name, is logged as a warning at startup.
- An invalid value, such as a `Duration` that isn't a positive time span, makes the host fail to start with an
  `InvalidOperationException` naming the setting (without a generic host, the first cached call throws). If a
  reloaded file has one, the reload is logged as an error and the previous policies stay.

## Runtime overrides

A runtime override of a method wins over that method's other layers (its attribute, startup code and
`appsettings.json`). Use them to change a policy without a deploy, for example to shorten a duration during an
incident:

```cs
var configurator = app.Services.GetRequiredService<IRuntimeCacheConfigurator>();

// One method, strongly typed, with who and why for the audit trail
await configurator.UpsertAsync<IOrdersService, Order>(
    s => s.GetAsync(Any<int>.Value),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)),
    new RuntimeOverrideMetadata(Owner: "ops", Reason: "Incident 4211", ExpiresAt: DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddHours(4)));

// By method id, for example from an admin form
await configurator.UpsertAsync("Docs.Configuration.IUserService.GetProfileAsync",
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)));

// Back to the lower layers
await configurator.RemoveAsync<IOrdersService, Order>(s => s.GetAsync(Any<int>.Value));
await configurator.ClearAsync();
```

| Method | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `UpsertAsync` | Adds or replaces the override for one method, by expression or method id |
| `UpsertBatchAsync` | Several overrides in one call |
| `ApplyAsync` | Overrides for the methods listed with `ForService<T>().Method(...)`, as in startup code |
| `RemoveAsync` / `ClearAsync` | Removes one override, or all of them |
| `GetOverridesAsync` / `GetOverrideAsync` | Returns the active overrides |
| `WatchAsync` | Streams override changes |

- Runtime defaults, `DefaultPolicy` or `ForGroup` inside `ApplyAsync`, are defaults like the ones in startup code:
  they fill in what a method leaves unset, and a method's own values, such as `[Cache(Duration = "01:00:00")]`, still
  win over them. To change one method, override that method.
- Tags in an override are added to the method's other tags; call `ClearTags()` first to replace them (see above).
- `RuntimeOverrideMetadata` (owner, reason, ticket, expiry) is kept with the override for auditing. An override stops
  applying when its `ExpiresAt` passes.
- Overrides are held in memory. They are lost on restart and not shared between instances.
- Concurrent changes apply in order: the latest one wins, also for removal, clearing and expiry.
- An override can't turn caching off: `WithDuration` requires a positive duration. To get rid of stale data,
  [invalidate](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md) it.

## Seeing the effective policy

`PolicyDiagnosticsService` (in `MethodCache.Policies`) shows each method's merged policy and which layers contributed:

```cs
var diagnostics = app.Services.GetRequiredService<PolicyDiagnosticsService>();

foreach (var report in diagnostics.GetAllPolicies())
{
    var sources = string.Join(", ", report.Contributions.Select(c => c.SourceId).Distinct());
    Console.WriteLine($"{report.MethodId}: Duration={report.Policy.Duration}, from {sources}");
}
```

`GetPolicy(methodId)` returns one method's report, and `FindBySource(sourceId)` the methods a layer configured. The
source ids are `attributes`, `startup-fluent`, `configuration-files` and `runtime-overrides`. The admin endpoint
`GET /methodcache/methods` shows the same ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

## Validation

| Setting | Rule | Checked |
|---------|------|---------|
| `Duration`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead` | A positive time span | `[Cache]`: at build time ([MC0004](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0004)). Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup |
| `FailSafe` | A positive time span or `"off"`; in code, `TimeSpan.Zero` turns it off | `[Cache]`: at build time ([MC0004](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0004)). Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a negative value. JSON: at startup |
| `FailSafeTimeout`, `FailSafeRetryAfter` | A positive time span | `[Cache]` (`FailSafeTimeout` only): at build time. Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup |
| `Version` | Zero or more | Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup. On `[Cache]`, a negative value means "not set" (the default is -1) |

`OnHit`, `OnMiss`, `WithMetrics` and `When` only apply to [manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md); configuring them for a
`[Cache]` method throws `InvalidOperationException` at startup instead of being silently ignored. "At startup" means
when the generic host starts (`app.Run()`, `host.StartAsync()`), which loads every policy source; with a plain
`BuildServiceProvider()`, the first cached call loads them and throws. To decide per result
whether a `[Cache]` method stores it, use [`CacheWhen`](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md#cachewhen).

Overloaded generic methods include generic arity in their policy ids and key prefixes: `Get(int)`, `Get``1(int)` and `Get``2(int)` remain distinct. Generator and runtime configuration use the same ids; earlier keys for overloaded generic methods become cold misses.

Policy tags are owned, read-only snapshots in both `CachePolicy` and `CacheRuntimePolicy`. Mutating the collection supplied by application code cannot change a published policy or bypass its version/change notifications.

A keyed `ICacheManager` registration remains independent of the default unkeyed manager. Registering another service key does not suppress `AddMethodCache()` or its default administration services.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/manual-caching.md -->

# Manual caching

When an attribute doesn't fit, such as a call in the middle of a method or a client without an interface, use the same
cache through `ICacheManager` with a key you choose:

```cs
public sealed class OrderReader(ICacheManager cache, IOrderRepository orders)
{
    public ValueTask<Order> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default) =>
        cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
            $"order:{id}",
            async (ctx, token) => await orders.GetAsync(id, token),
            o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)).WithTags("orders", $"order:{id}"),
            cancellationToken: ct);
}
```

It shares the in-memory cache, the distributed cache, stampede protection and invalidation with `[Cache]` methods.

## Keys

You always pass the key yourself. MethodCache doesn't derive keys from the lambda, so a captured variable never ends
up in a key by accident, and two calls share an entry only when their keys are equal. Use a prefix per kind of data,
such as `order:42`, so keys from different places can't collide. An empty or whitespace key throws
`ArgumentException`.

## Options

`GetOrCreateAsync` takes every option, including callbacks and a predicate that only make sense per call:

```cs
var list = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"orders:{customerId}:{status}",
    async (ctx, ct) => await orders.ListAsync(customerId, status, ct),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30))
          .WithSlidingExpiration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10))
          .RefreshAhead(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5))
          .WithTags("orders", $"customer:{customerId}")
          .WithVersion(2)
          .OnHit(ctx => logger.LogDebug("Cache hit: {Key}", ctx.Key))
          .OnMiss(ctx => logger.LogDebug("Cache miss: {Key}", ctx.Key))
          .When(ctx => customerId > 0));   // skip the cache when false
```

- Duration, sliding expiration, refresh-ahead, tags and version work as described in [Expiration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md) and
  [Invalidation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md).
- `When` skips the cache for this call when it returns false ([Conditional caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md)).
- `OnHit`, `OnMiss` and `WithMetrics` observe this call. The `CacheContext` they get carries the key, an `Items`
  dictionary scoped to the call and `Services`, the `services` argument of `GetOrCreateAsync` (null when you don't
  pass one).
- These policies live in code: `appsettings.json` and runtime overrides apply to `[Cache]` methods only. `When`,
  `OnHit`, `OnMiss` and `WithMetrics` work here only ([Validation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#validation)).
- `CacheEntryOptions.Builder.Build()` takes a copy of the tags and callbacks, so changing the builder afterwards
  doesn't change options already built.

## Reading without loading

```cs
var lookup = await cache.TryGetAsync<Order>("order:42");
if (lookup.Found)
{
    Console.WriteLine(lookup.Value);
}
```

`TryGetAsync` takes the same `version` an entry was stored with.

## Versions and the stored key

An entry stored with `WithVersion` lives under a different key than the unversioned one: `entry` at version 1 never
shares a value with the key `entry::v1`. Keys that begin with a NUL character are escaped too. `CacheContext.Key`
always holds the key you passed. To invalidate or look up such an entry directly, for example with
`InvalidateByKeysAsync` or `ICacheAdministrator`, get the stored key from `CacheManagerExtensions.GetCacheKey(key,
version)` (leave out `version` for an unversioned entry) instead of building it by hand.

## Many keys at once

Key, tag and clear invalidation also guard the batch factory while it reads its source. Its caller can receive the in-flight result, but invalidated candidates are not published into memory or the distributed cache. Individual callers can still load and publish these keys during the batch; a fresh concurrent value wins.

`GetOrCreateManyAsync` checks the local cache for every key, looks up the local misses in the distributed cache,
and calls the factory once with the keys neither holds. Each key gets the value the cache selects: memory first, then
the distributed cache, then the factory. A bulk read therefore agrees with individual reads of the same keys, even
across nodes: a value another node stored in the distributed cache is returned as is, and its key is not passed to
the factory. A concurrent writer may still win over a value the factory produced; the returned dictionary then holds
the writer's value, as an individual read would:

```cs
var users = await cache.GetOrCreateManyAsync<User>(
    userIds.Select(id => $"user:{id}"),
    async (missingKeys, ctx, ct) =>
    {
        var ids = missingKeys.Select(k => int.Parse(k["user:".Length..])).ToList();
        var loaded = await repository.GetUsersAsync(ids, ct);   // one query for all misses
        return loaded.ToDictionary(u => $"user:{u.Id}", u => u);
    },
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromHours(1)));
```

## Things to know

- Concurrent calls for the same key share one factory run. A caller's `cancellationToken` stops its own wait; if it
  cancels a run others joined, they run the factory again rather than fail.
- A factory that asks for the key it is loading (itself, or through the cached service it belongs to) would wait for
  itself, so that call throws an `InvalidOperationException` instead, and the key is free for the next caller.
- To cache a sequence, materialize it in the factory (`await query.ToListAsync(ct)`) and cache the list.
- `GetOrCreateAsync` is an extension method, so mocking libraries can't intercept it. In tests, pass a
  `NoOpCacheManager` ([Testing](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/testing.md)).

Manual `TryGetAsync` reads a fresh entry, including a cached null, even when the fast path is disabled or refresh-ahead is due. This lookup does not start a factory or background refresh.

An explicit `SetAsync` with a lifetime shorter than L2 millisecond precision removes the previous distributed value instead of leaving it readable. If the backend is unavailable, the removal follows the normal invalidation retry path.

Caller cancellation stops the wait during an L2 read or a slow factory, including bulk reads and fail-safe waits. Shared work may finish for other callers; cancellation is not reported as a dependency failure.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/third-party.md -->

# Caching third-party code

MethodCache can cache calls to code you don't own, such as API clients, cloud SDKs or payment gateways, to cut API
costs and latency. Pick one of three approaches:

| Approach | Best for |
|----------|----------|
| `[assembly: CacheInterface]` | A client that ships an interface: cache chosen methods with one line, no wrapper |
| A wrapper interface with `[Cache]` | A client without an interface (a sealed class or static methods) |
| `ICacheManager.GetOrCreateAsync` | One or two calls, or keys you want to build yourself |

## The client's own interface

Name the interface and the methods to cache in an assembly attribute, anywhere in your project:

```cs
[assembly: CacheInterface(typeof(IFxRatesClient), nameof(IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync),
    Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFxRatesClient, FxRatesClient>();   // the vendor's client, registered as usual
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

- The listed methods behave like methods with `[Cache]`: keys from the arguments, tag templates with the method's
  parameter names, zero-allocation hits on .NET 9 and later. Methods you don't list always reach the client, so writes
  are never cached by accident.
- The attribute's settings (`Duration`, `Tags`, `Group`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`, `Version`, `FailSafe`,
  `FailSafeTimeout`) apply to every listed method. Give one method its own settings like any cached method:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config => config.Method((IFxRatesClient c) => c.GetRateAsync(Any<string>.Value, Any<string>.Value))
    .Configure(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))));
```

- The method id in `appsettings.json` and the admin endpoints is the interface's full name, a dot and the method name,
  for example `FxVendor.IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync`.
- List each interface once. It must be non-generic and come from another assembly; for your own interfaces, put
  `[Cache]` on the methods. A method with overloads can't be listed yet.
- The attribute can live in a class library, such as your infrastructure project. `AddMethodCache()` finds it in
  every loaded assembly that references MethodCache, even when none of the library's code has run yet. The runtime
  loads a library when code that uses one of its types runs, so a library your application never uses in code is
  not searched; registering one of its types, or `typeof` of one, is enough.
- When a library you use lists the same interface too, each assembly has its own decorator and policies.
  `AddMethodCache()` uses the one generated in the assemblies passed to it (by default the calling one, usually your
  application), then the one in the entry assembly. If neither has one, it throws `InvalidOperationException` naming
  both; pass the assembly whose policies should apply: `AddMethodCache(null, typeof(Program).Assembly)`.
- Mistakes are build errors: [MCG010](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg010) (a type it can't cache, such as one with
  static abstract or non-public abstract members), [MCG011](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg011) (a method that is
  missing, overloaded, static, or one `[Cache]` would reject) and [MCG012](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mcg012) (an
  interface listed twice).

## A wrapper interface

Define an interface in your project with the calls you need, and put the settings on it:

```cs
public interface IRates
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
    Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to);
}

public sealed class Rates(FxRatesClient client) : IRates   // calls the vendor's concrete class
{
    public Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to) => client.GetRateAsync(from, to);
}
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<FxRatesClient>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRates, Rates>();
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

Static methods and sealed classes work the same way: the wrapper calls them, and the interface carries the attributes.

## An explicit key

```cs
var rate = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"fx:{from}:{to}",
    async (ctx, ct) => await client.GetRateAsync(from, to),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)).WithTags("fx"));
```

See [Manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md).

## Things to know

- **Leave writes uncached.** Payments, uploads and deletes must not be cached; mark wrapper methods that change data
  with `[CacheInvalidate(Tags = ...)]`.
- **Exceptions are not cached.** With [fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md) on, the previous value is served while the client
  fails.
- **Invalidate from a webhook** with `cache.InvalidateByTagsAsync("fx:EUR")` when the vendor tells you data changed.
- **Share results between instances** with a [distributed cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md) when every instance calls the
  same paid API.
- **Start with short durations** and lengthen them once you know how fresh the data must be.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/http-caching.md -->

# HTTP response caching

Add `AddHttpCaching()` to an `HttpClient` registration to cache HTTP responses according to their response headers,
as RFC 9111 describes. Freshness comes from `Cache-Control` and expiry headers; `ETag` and `Last-Modified` enable
conditional validation, and a successful 304 is returned to the caller as the full response.

```cs
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IGitHubClient, GitHubClient>()
    .AddHttpCaching();
```

The [package guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.HttpCaching/README.md) covers settings, storage, private and shared caches,
limits and metrics. This page covers the rules the cache follows and how to write your own storage. See
[Security](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/security.md#methodcachehttpcaching) for the threat model.

A full replacement response also retires the previous cached representation when it cannot be stored, including `no-store`, shared-cache `private`, a body over the size limit, or a failed replacement write. The next caller cannot fall back to an older fresh body. Stale-while-revalidate respects explicit request `max-age`, `min-fresh` and `max-stale` limits.

Concurrent writers with the same variant selection share its namespace, including across processes using distributed storage. The body-free variant index is retained for the maximum supported response lifetime (365 days); individual variants still expire at their own TTL. A change to the selecting headers retires the URL publication epoch exactly once; a concurrent response published after that retirement remains reachable; the current response reaches its caller, and the next request fetches and stores the new schema. If deleting the old entry fails after the epoch was rotated, foreground validation reports that error without rotating again; background validation logs it. A concurrent publication in the new epoch remains reachable.

## Freshness and validation

- Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error are optional. Response `no-cache` requires successful validation before
  the response is reused, even when either option is on. Request `no-cache` has the same requirement: a 5xx response
  or network error reaches the caller rather than falling back to cached content.
- `must-revalidate` forbids serving a stale response, as do `proxy-revalidate` and `s-maxage` in a shared cache.
- An `Expires` at or before the response `Date`, or one that doesn't parse (such as `Expires: 0`), makes the response
  stale at once. Heuristic freshness and `DefaultMaxAge` don't extend it. An explicit `max-age` (or `s-maxage` in a
  shared cache) wins over `Expires`.
- A 304 updates the stored response's headers and whether it may be stored. If it changes to `no-store`, `Vary: *`, or
  `private` in a shared cache, the stored response is removed. This applies to background revalidation too. A 304
  without `Vary` keeps the original variant selection. If the updated response can't be stored, the old one is
  removed so its old rules are never used again; the caller still gets the response. If removing it fails too, the
  error reaches the caller.
- A `Cache-Control` or `Vary` field that doesn't parse (such as `private; max-age=600` or `max-age=-1`), also next to a valid one, is not
  read as absent: the response is not stored, because the header may have said `private` or `no-store`.
- An entry is kept at most a year, even when `Expires` is far in the future (`31 Dec 9999`).
- Weak ETags (`W/"abc"`) are sent back as weak validators.
- `only-if-cached` never contacts the origin, including for range requests, requests with their own validators,
  `no-store`, methods that aren't cached and background revalidation. When no stored response can be used, the
  answer is 504.

## Redirects, retries and request bodies

- A redirect the transport follows (`AllowAutoRedirect`, the default) answers a different URL, so it is not stored
  under the URL you requested. The transport also drops `Authorization` on a redirect, so storing it could hand one
  caller's response to another. Requests that end at the redirect target are cached under that URL as usual. If the
  target answers the cache's own validators with 304, the request is sent again without them, so you get the full response.
  A URL that was cached and now redirects has its stored response removed, also when background revalidation finds out.
- The cache stores responses for the request as you sent it, before the transport adds headers such as
  `Accept-Encoding` for automatic decompression. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` therefore works with `AutomaticDecompression`.
- The `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` headers the cache adds are removed again before the response is
  returned, so a retry handler (Polly, standard resilience) that sends the same message again gets a full response.
- A `GET` or `HEAD` with a body (search APIs such as Elasticsearch) goes to the origin: its URL doesn't identify it.
- The URL fragment (`#top`) is not part of the key; it never reaches the origin.

## Writes and invalidation

A successful `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` starts a new cache generation for its URL before it returns. That is
the URL you sent it to, also when the response redirects (`303 See Other`) elsewhere. A GET or
background revalidation that was already in flight can still complete, but it stores its response under the old
generation, so later requests fetch the updated response. With `UseDistributedCache` the generation is shared by
every instance.

The built-in storage groups URLs into 4096 generation slots per storage prefix, so its metadata stays bounded. Two
URLs that share a slot can cause an extra cache miss when either is invalidated. Generation records never expire on
their own; if the backend evicts one anyway, the next request starts a new generation, so a lost record only causes
cache misses and never brings back a response from before a write. If reading the generation fails, the request goes
to the origin. If storing a new generation fails, the error reaches the caller, although the write to the origin may
already have succeeded.

## Custom storage

To store responses somewhere else, implement `IHttpCacheStorage`. A successful write calls only `InvalidateAsync`,
and responses are looked up under the generation from `GetGenerationAsync`, so both must be correct:

- Every invalidation publishes a new generation, unique and shared by every storage instance. A storage that returns
  a constant generation, or implements `InvalidateAsync` as a no-op, keeps serving old responses after a write.
- A generation value is never reused. A missing or lost generation record starts a new unique one, never one used
  before. Several keys may share a generation.
- Clearing the storage also changes generations, so a request still in flight can't store an older response into
  the active generation.

A minimal correct storage:

```cs
public sealed class DictionaryHttpCacheStorage(TimeProvider time) : IHttpCacheStorage
{
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, (HttpCacheEntry Entry, DateTimeOffset Expires)> _entries = new();
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, string> _generations = new();

    // Responses are stored per generation. A missing generation (never set, cleared or lost) starts a new
    // unique one, never a value used before, so losing it can only cause cache misses.
```
